findings.reason: Lines 287-292 call SetOriginalValue(property, this[property]) for every Throw property, with no restriction to complex types or shadow properties. EntityEntry.State's setter (EntityEntry.cs:86) calls SetEntityState directly without running DetectChanges. The trace: tracked entity, change a Throw property, then State=Modified or Update. The original now equals the new value, so the guard at InternalEntryBase.cs:1655-1661 never sees IsModified and does not throw.
findings.claim: Every AfterSaveBehavior.Throw property (keys included) has its original value overwritten with the current value whenever an entry is set to Modified. A change to a read-only property on a tracked entity is then dropped silently, or for keys the UPDATE targets the new key, instead of raising PropertyReadOnlyAfterSave.
findings.evidence: Trigger: for an entity tracked as Unchanged, `var entry = ctx.Entry(e); e.ReadOnlyProp = "x"; entry.State = EntityState.Modified; ctx.SaveChanges();`. The `EntityEntry.State` setter (EntityEntry.cs:78-87) calls `InternalEntry.SetEntityState(value)` directly and does not run DetectChanges. SetEntityState now runs `SetOriginalValue(property, this[property], skipChangeDetection: true)` for every Throw property (lines 287-292), so the original snapshot becomes "x". DetectChanges in SaveChanges then finds no difference, the property is never flagged Modified, and the guard at InternalEntryBase.cs:1655-1661 (`GetAfterSaveBehavior() == Throw && IsModified(property)` throws PropertyReadOnlyAfterSave) never fires. The update is dropped without any error. `entry.OriginalValues` also now reports the new value, which misleads auditing code and interceptors. No other check takes over the guard's job on this path.

members.claim: This overwrites the original value of every AfterSaveBehavior.Throw property whenever an entry goes to Modified with modifyProperties. That includes primary/alternate key properties and entity discriminators, not just the complex-type shadow discriminator in the bug. Suppose a tracked Unchanged entity has a key or other read-only property changed and is then set to `entry.State = EntityState.Modified` before DetectChanges runs (for example with AutoDetectChanges off). Before this change, DetectChanges/SaveChanges caught the change and threw. Now the original is silently replaced with the new value. For keys, the UPDATE's WHERE clause uses the original key value, so the update can hit a different row or none. For other Throw properties, the change is dropped silently instead of producing the documented exception. The fix should be limited to properties whose snapshot is known to be wrong (the complex-type shadow default case), or the snapshot itself should be fixed.

members.claim: Preserve original values for already-tracked read-only properties
members.evidence: For an already-tracked entity, changing a non-key property configured with `AfterSaveBehavior.Throw` and then calling `Update(entity)` now replaces its original value with the changed value. Consequently, `DetectChanges` no longer detects the illegal modification, and `SaveChanges` silently succeeds while leaving the database value unchanged. This also corrupts the original-value snapshot exposed to callers. Limit the snapshot correction to the disconnected complex-type discriminator scenario rather than applying it to every read-only property on every transition to Modified.

findings.reason: SnapshotFactoryFactory.cs:132-136 still writes GetDefaultValueConstant() for shadow properties on complex types, and that is the cause the new comment names. The workaround only runs when newState==Modified with modifyProperties, so the snapshot defect remains on other paths, and the broad condition is what causes the high regression. I did not run the Attach path end to end.
findings.claim: The fix patches the symptom in the Modified state transition. The real cause is the snapshot storing defaults for shadow properties on complex types, and it is left in place, so other paths (e.g. Attach followed by DetectChanges) can still hit the false mismatch.
findings.evidence: The added comment names the cause itself: "for shadow properties on complex types whose snapshot stores default values". But the condition `afterSaveBehavior == PropertySaveBehavior.Throw && property.GetOriginalValueIndex() >= 0 && !IsConceptualNull(property)` is not limited to complex types, shadow properties or discriminators. It runs for every Modified transition with modifyProperties, including on ordinary entity keys. That is the source of the regression above.

members.claim: This treats the symptom, not the root cause: the snapshot factory (regression from #37394) stores default values for shadow properties on complex types instead of the current values. The same false mismatch still happens on other paths. For example, with Attach() followed by DetectChanges, the entry is Unchanged, this block never runs, and the complex discriminator is still flagged as modified, so SaveChanges throws. Shadow Save properties on complex types would also be falsely flagged as modified. The more targeted snapshot fix (#38111) addresses the actual defect without changing state-transition semantics for every entity type.

findings.reason: The overwrite is unconditional: lines 269-292 run even when oldState==newState, before the early return at 312. So an original value set explicitly on a Throw property is lost. A concurrency token configured as Throw is an unusual setup, though, since tokens are typically Ignore/value-generated, and the code doesn't show how common it is. Lowered from high to medium.
findings.claim: Throw properties that are also concurrency tokens, or original values the user set explicitly through OriginalValues, are clobbered by the current value when state is set to Modified (including Modified->Modified).
findings.evidence: Throw properties that are also concurrency tokens lose their real original value. SetEntityState(Modified) is also reached for Modified->Modified transitions (calling Update/State=Modified again) and for Unchanged->Modified on entities loaded from the database. In those cases the database-loaded original value, which the UPDATE's concurrency check uses in its WHERE clause, is replaced with the current in-memory value. This can hide concurrency conflicts or cause wrong rows to be matched. Any original value the user set explicitly through `entry.OriginalValues` before changing state is also clobbered.
